content: For children aged 5 years and older who are clinically stable and/or have achieved viral suppression on antiretroviral therapy (ART) for at least six months, and have a CD4 count greater than 350 cells/mm³, continuation of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is strongly recommended, although the evidence supporting this is of very low certainty. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is also recommended for HIV-exposed infants starting from 4 to 6 weeks of age and should be continued until HIV infection is definitively excluded through age-appropriate testing after breastfeeding has ceased. This recommendation is also strong but based on very low certainty evidence. Additionally, routine co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is advised for all individuals living with HIV who have tuberculosis (TB), regardless of their CD4 cell count, supported by strong evidence of high certainty. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes that ART in children and adolescents living with HIV aims to improve both the quality and length of life, reduce HIV-related morbidity and mortality, lower the incidence of opportunistic infections (including TB), suppress viral load, and restore immune function, as well as support normal growth and development. ART has also been shown to improve TB treatment outcomes in this population. WHO recommends initiating ART in all children and adolescents living with HIV, regardless of their clinical stage or CD4 count. Rapid initiation of ART, ideally within seven days of confirmed HIV diagnosis and clinical assessment, is encouraged, with same-day initiation offered to those ready to start. Priority should be given to children and adolescents with advanced HIV disease. ART initiation should follow principles of people-centered care, which respects individual dignity, preferences, and informed decision-making, while supporting active participation in care. For children and adolescents with TB, ART should be started as soon as possible, ideally within two weeks of initiating TB treatment, regardless of CD4 count, unless signs of meningitis are present. In cases of TB meningitis, ART initiation should be delayed by at least four weeks but started within eight weeks of TB treatment initiation. Corticosteroids, such as dexamethasone or prednisolone tapered over 6–8 weeks, may be considered as adjunctive therapy for TB meningitis. Regarding ART regimens, dolutegravir (DTG) is approved for use in children over 4 weeks of age and weighing more than 3 kg, with a dispersible 10 mg formulation available. For children where DTG dosing is not approved, raltegravir (RAL) is an effective alternative and is approved from birth, with dose adjustments required during TB treatment. RAL should be replaced with DTG as soon as it becomes available. DTG combined with a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) backbone is the preferred first-line regimen for adolescents and children starting ART. Low-dose efavirenz (EFV 400 mg) with an NRTI backbone is an alternative first-line regimen for adolescents, except in settings with high levels of pre-treatment resistance to EFV or nevirapine (NVP). If DTG is unavailable, a lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r)-based regimen is preferred. RAL should only be used in special circumstances, such as in neonates, and transitioned to DTG as soon as possible. For individuals with TB/HIV co-infection, adjustments to ART regimens may be necessary. For example, the dose of DTG should be doubled (administered twice daily) due to drug-drug interactions with rifampicin. Similarly, RAL dosing should be increased to 800 mg twice daily instead of 400 mg twice daily when co-administered with rifamycins. Rifampicin and rifapentine can be co-administered with EFV or DTG without dose adjustments, but they should not be used with protease inhibitors or NVP due to significant drug interactions. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), a temporary clinical deterioration that may occur within three months of starting ART, is a recognized complication. It is most common within the first month of ART initiation and is associated with immune recovery, characterized by an increase in CD4 count and suppression of viral load. IRIS can manifest as a paradoxical worsening of treated infections or the unmasking of previously subclinical infections, particularly TB. Risk factors for IRIS include low baseline CD4 count, disseminated TB, early ART initiation, and rapid immunological and virological responses to ART. While IRIS can cause significant morbidity, it is not typically associated with increased mortality. Management of IRIS may involve the use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for mild to moderate cases or corticosteroids for severe cases, except in cases of drug-resistant TB. ART should generally be continued unless IRIS is life-threatening or likely to cause permanent disability. In pregnant women, TB contributes significantly to maternal mortality and adverse pregnancy outcomes, including pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, miscarriage, and low birth weight. TB in pregnancy also increases the risk of vertical HIV transmission. Prompt initiation of TB treatment is critical to prevent transmission. The treatment of TB in pregnant women is the same as in non-pregnant women, and all pregnant women with TB/HIV co-infection are eligible for ART. Screening for TB should be integrated into antenatal care, particularly in regions endemic for TB and HIV. Congenital TB, acquired in utero or during delivery, typically presents within the first three weeks of life and has a high mortality rate. Management of congenital and neonatal TB is the same and should be overseen by a clinician experienced in pediatric TB. Treatment should be initiated promptly based on clinical suspicion, even before bacteriological confirmation, as TB can progress rapidly in neonates. Breastfeeding is recommended regardless of the mother’s TB status, as the risk of transmission through breast milk is negligible. For asymptomatic neonates born to mothers with TB, TB disease should be excluded, and preventive treatment should be provided once TB disease is ruled out. BCG vaccination should be delayed until after the completion of preventive treatment. Neonates exposed to multidrug-resistant TB should be referred to a specialist for management.
